Self-limiting Success

 

When Warren Buffett stepped down last week as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, readers flocked to The Wall Street Journal story reporting the news.

 

Many clicked because Buffett is so famous. Others are Berkshire shareholders and wondered what it meant for them. Most, though, follow news about Buffett because they hope that a little bit of his secret sauce will rub off on them.

 

He’s certainly a worthy role model but, his age aside, not even Buffett could keep being like himself. You’re probably younger, but you also don’t own a time machine. The Journal’s Jason Zweig points out that Buffett “fed on the tiniest plankton of the stock market” in his heyday, buying stakes in unloved, small companies. 

 

Those days are over.

 

Then there’s math. Even if you lived as long as Methuselah, it’s impossible to keep growing a pile of capital using a very sound strategy because success is self-limiting.

 

Say an investment fund at the turn of the 20th Century had figured out decades ahead of time the value and quality factors that worked so well for Buffett. Earning as much as him, around 20% annually, the fund would have grown $10,000 into $100 trillion today—triple the size of the U.S. economy. There would be nobody left to beat to keep those returns going.

 

As Berkshire’s value passed a mere $1 trillion, its returns have looked pedestrian and it has built up the biggest cash hoard in history. It’s hard to find investments that can move the needle at that size. 

 

Having too much money isn’t a problem for anyone reading this, but there are other obstacles to making Buffett-like returns. Academics have tried to distill its essence, most famously in a paper called “Buffett’s Alpha.” Somehow there aren’t other Berkshires around.

 

Hacks that even Buffett couldn’t use get competed away quickly these days as other smart people find out about them. Meanwhile, value and quality have hit a rough patch, making them hard to stick with.

 

If you have the ability to latch on to a superior strategy and close your eyes then that could earn you an extra percentage point or two in the long run. Or it might not. A plethora of exchange-traded funds now offer affordable ways to try.

 

But if doing better than your peers is enough then that’s close to a sure thing. It even gives you a way to be like Buffett—sort of. His will calls for his widow to invest 90% of her inheritance in an S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short-term Treasurys.

 

The typical overactive investor trails that simple portfolio by about 1.5 percentage points a year.

 

Where does all their foregone wealth go? That’s why there are people like Warren Buffett.
